# Conservative Party Manifesto 2005 Summary

## The British Dream

The Conservatives present Britain as a great nation with tremendous potential—creative, enterprising, tolerant and freedom-loving—but one heading in the wrong direction under Labour. The manifesto argues that hardworking families who "do the right thing" are being taken for granted rather than rewarded, while everyday frustrations in healthcare, education, crime and immigration prevent people from fulfilling their potential.

The Conservatives pledge to govern with different values: extending choice to individuals, devolving power from Whitehall to communities, trusting professionals, and focusing on practical priorities—cleaner hospitals, school discipline, more police, controlled immigration and lower taxes.

## Key Policy Areas

**Economy and Taxes**: The Conservatives criticise Labour's excessive spending, waste and "stealth taxes." They pledge to cut £12 billion through efficiency savings—freezing civil service recruitment, removing 235,000 bureaucratic posts—while maintaining NHS and schools funding. They will use savings to reduce borrowing and deliver £4 billion in tax cuts, including halving council tax for pensioners and linking state pensions to earnings.

**Education**: Promising discipline and standards, Conservatives would give head teachers full control over admissions and expulsions, sending disruptive pupils to "Turnaround Schools." They pledge rigorous examinations, reduced paperwork for teachers, and parental choice—including funding for children to attend independent schools. They oppose the "dogmatic pursuit of inclusion" that has closed special schools.

**Healthcare**: The manifesto promises to match Labour's NHS spending while cutting bureaucracy and abolishing centrally-set targets. Hospitals would gain freedom to manage locally, matrons would return with power to close wards for cleaning, and patients would receive genuine choice over providers.

**Crime**: Describing crime as "out of control," Conservatives pledge 5,000 additional police officers annually, genuine neighbourhood policing, 20,000 extra prison places, and honest sentencing so criminals serve full terms. They would reclassify cannabis back to Class B and massively expand drug treatment programmes.

**Immigration**: The Conservatives argue Labour has "lost effective control of our borders." They would establish a British Border Control Police, introduce an Australian-style points system for work permits, withdraw from the 1951 Geneva Convention, and set annual limits on immigration including asylum quotas.

## Constitutional Reform

The manifesto promises English votes for English laws, abolition of regional assemblies, a 20 per cent reduction in MPs, and a referendum on the EU Constitution—campaigning for "no." They oppose Euro membership and pledge to restore the opt-out from the European Social Chapter.

## Conclusion

The Conservatives frame this election as a choice between "another five years of talk" under Blair or "action" on issues mattering to "hardworking Britons"—a Government that rewards those who "do the right thing."
